4. Contracts

Say a colleague's transformation feeds the billing job you own. Its docstring promises that the new column is never negative and never NULL, and customers are invoiced on that promise. You would like it proved. In verified programming a function states what it requires of its inputs (preconditions) and what it ensures about its output (postconditions), and a machine proves the second follows from the first. Sverify does this for a data transformation: a function from Ibis tables to an Ibis table, with a decorator that states the contract. This chapter covers the contract itself, keys and relations between columns, runtime errors, windows and composing contracts. The proofs are described in how it works.

A first contract

We'll write one.

data.text/html:
proved
semantics: reference
postcondition status
(_.doubled >= 0) ✅ proved
_.doubled.notnull() ✅ proved
id IS NOT NULL ✅ proved
output column known values
id any integer
doubled an integer in [22, 1999999998]

data.text/markdown:
• requires maps each parameter of the function to conditions on that input. ensures lists conditions on the output.
  • Conditions are Ibis expressions over the table's columns (_.amount >= 0, using Ibis's _ placeholder) or SQL snippets ("id IS NOT NULL").
  • Calling doubled(orders) builds the Ibis expression as usual. Before returning it, sverify sends the plan and the conditions to the Lean checker (substrait-check --contract), which tries to prove every postcondition. The verdicts are in .report.
  • The first table of the report holds the verdicts. The second holds everything Lean established about each output column, asked for or not.
  • amount < 1_000_000_000 is there for amount * 2. Doubling the largest 64-bit integer overflows and the reference raises, so the plan needs an upper bound on amount. Without one, Sverify works out the weakest, amount < 2**62, and reports the plan as not proved until you declare a bound. Like every precondition, it is checked on your data, or proved from table metadata.
sv.verify(expr, requires=..., ensures=...) does the same for an expression without a decorator and returns the report.

How Lean knows doubled ≥ 22

Lean runs the plan on descriptions of values: for each column, whether it can be NULL and which values it can hold. This is abstract interpretation, and each operator updates the descriptions.
  • The preconditions make amount >= 0 and amount < 1_000_000_000 TRUE on every input row, so amount is a non-NULL integer in [0, 10⁹ - 1]. (NULL >= 0 is NULL, which is not TRUE.)
  • The filter amount > 10 keeps the rows where that is TRUE, so amount is a non-NULL integer ≥ 11 afterwards.
  • amount * 2 is then an integer in [22, 2·10⁹ - 2], which fits in 64 bits and is never NULL.
A postcondition is proved when its description allows only TRUE.

When a proof fails

A promise that does not follow is refused, together with what Lean could establish. Here the precondition allows amount = 0, so total can be 1:

VerificationError: 1 of 1 postcondition not proved, 1 precondition needed (e.report has the details)
  needs: (_.amount < 9 * 10**18) on orders, inferred from `amount + 1` (overflow otherwise): declare it in requires (each run then checks it on the data), or rewrite so no row needs it (`orders.filter((_.amount < 9 * 10**18))` first, or a CASE); on_inferred='warn' assumes it instead
  not proved: (_.total > 5): it may be FALSE on some rows (counterexample: orders(id, customer, amount) = [(0, '', 0)] gives (id, total) = [(0, 1)])
    would hold with `(_.amount >= 5)` in the requires of 'orders'

"It may be FALSE on some rows" is Lean's answer when total > 5 holds for some allowed inputs and fails for others. A refusal can also mean the truth is out of reach of the analysis (the list at the end of this section says what it tracks), so a refusal means "not proved".

Contracts on real data

So far the table had no data, and the proof covered every possible orders. Real tables come from upstream systems, and binding the function to one adds two things.
  1. Preconditions are checked on the data at call time, because they are assumptions about the outside world. A violation raises PreconditionError.
  2. An unproved postcondition can be checked on the output instead of refusing the call, with on_unproved.
on_unproved= what happens when a postcondition is not proved
"error" (default) VerificationError; nothing runs
"check" the pipeline runs and the condition is checked on the output; a violation raises PostconditionError
"warn" a warning, and the pipeline runs
Take a table with a NULL in it and the condition amount < 100, which nothing bounds, so it is not proved. With "check" the pipeline runs and the condition is checked on the output.

data.text/markdown: The check fails for cy's row: NULL < 100 is not TRUE, so the NULL counts as a violation. A contract condition must be TRUE. A precondition amount >= 0 would fail first, for the same NULL, and check_requires=False on sv.transform trusts the inputs, so that the proofs rest on that trust. A column declared non-nullable ("!int64" in Ibis) is never NULL, and Lean knows it, so amount IS NOT NULL needs no precondition.

What backs a proof

Theorem contract_sound in analysis/Sverify/Analysis/Contracts.lean says: if every input row matches its schema and satisfies the preconditions, and the abstract interpretation says every postcondition is certainly TRUE, then every postcondition is TRUE on every output row. Sverify checks the hypotheses about the data when the data is there.

What Lean tracks

Per column: whether it can be NULL, integer and double ranges, timestamps, which booleans it can be, and which strings it can be while they are few. Filters such as amount > 10, x = 3, x IN (1, 2, 3), status <> 'cancelled' and x IS NOT NULL refine those facts. Arithmetic, comparisons, AND/OR/NOT with SQL's NULL semantics, CASE, COALESCE, joins and UNION ALL carry them through. Keys and relations between columns come next. Not tracked yet: relations that need more than a column plus a constant (a < 2 * b), what is inside a string and counts across rows. For those, on_unproved="check" checks the condition on the data.

Keys

Say you add each customer's city to the orders so finance can sum revenue by city. If a customer appears twice in customers, their orders are counted twice, and the totals stop matching the ledger. sv.unique("id") says the listed columns identify a row. In requires it is an assumption about an input, checked on the data when the input is bound. In ensures it is proved: keys survive filters and projections, and joins whose condition pins down at most one partner on the other side. We'll join orders with customers, with and without a key on the customer names.

data.text/markdown: Without the key on name, Lean refuses. Say Bob moved and was entered twice, once per city: his one order then appears twice and finance's totals are off by his 5. With the key in requires, a contracted function stops at the precondition check before finance sees a number.

data.text/markdown:
Keys come from other places too, all proved in analysis/Sverify/Analysis/Keys.lean (Rel.keys_sound).
  • DISTINCT rows are a key: all their columns together.
  • Semi and anti joins keep the left side's keys.
  • A filter x = 3 drops x from a key: unique(id, customer) and customer = 'ada' give unique(id).
  • ROW_NUMBER() with the partition columns is a key (see Windows below).
  • sv.references("cust", to=("customers", "id")) in requires says every non-NULL cust occurs in customers.id. It is an assumption, checked on the data, and nothing proves it in ensures.

data.text/markdown:
Foreign keys and row caps

An order for a customer who isn't in customers drops out of the join, and its revenue with it. sv.references states that every customer an order names exists, and sv.key is a key whose columns are never NULL. We'll add an order for Cy, whom customers doesn't know:

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003ePreconditionError: 1 row(s) of orders violate references(customer, customers.name)\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"danger"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown: Cy's order is caught before the join drops it. Nothing proves a foreign key in ensures: it stays a precondition, checked on the data. A row cap works the other way round. sv.max_rows(n) in requires is checked on the data, and Lean carries it through the plan (Rel.maxRows_sound). With it, a sum of amounts per customer is proved to fit 64 bits, and the cap on the output is proved too. Without it, the report assumes the sum fits and checks it as the job runs:

Relations between columns

Filter and join conditions such as a.t = b.t + 1, start < end or value != -9999 become facts about each row. The facts survive projections, joins and unions, and postconditions such as t1 - t0 == 1 or t1 > t0 follow from them. Say you prepare training data for a forecasting model. Readings arrive once a minute and -9999 marks a sensor error. Whoever trains the model assumes each pair is exactly one minute apart and that no -9999 slipped through. We'll prove both for a pipeline that joins the clean readings with themselves, one minute apart.

data.text/html:
NOT proved: 1 precondition needed
semantics: reference
postcondition status
((_.t1 - _.t0) == 1) ✅ proved
(_.t1 > _.t0) ✅ proved
(_.v0 != -9999) ✅ proved
(_.v1 != -9999) ✅ proved
unique(t0) ✅ proved
needs ❌ (_.minute < 9 * 10**18) on readings, inferred from minute + 1 (overflow otherwise): declare it in requires (each run then checks it on the data), or rewrite so no row needs it (readings.filter((_.minute < 9 * 10**18)) first, or a CASE); on_inferred='warn' assumes it instead
output column known values
t0 any integer
t1 any integer
v0 any integer
v1 any integer

data.text/markdown:
What each switch does:
  • minute IS NOT NULL: without it, t1 - t0 == 1 is "TRUE or NULL". The join condition w1.minute = w0.minute + 1 is TRUE only for non-NULL values, but Lean derives that for plain column comparisons and not through the + 1. When Lean sees no reason, it says so.
  • unique(sensor, minute): one reading per sensor and minute. Within sensor a that makes minute a key, and the join finds at most one t1 per t0, so unique(t0) holds.
  • Only sensor a: with several sensors the join also pairs readings of different sensors, because sensor is not in the join condition, and t0 repeats. The relations still hold, since they are about each row.
The facts are Expr.factsOf_sound and Rel.facts_sound in analysis/Sverify/Analysis/Contracts.lean: a fact x − y ∈ [lo, hi] or x ≠ k taken from a condition holds on every row that passes it, and every operator above keeps it.

Runtime errors

Say you are on call this week. At 3 a.m. a pipeline that was correct crashes on a row nobody expected, and it pages you. A pipeline that quietly writes a wrong number is worse, because nobody gets paged. Some operations can fail. The reference raises on each of these, and the report lists every one a plan may hit (Runtime errors).
  • Integer / or % by zero, and -9223372036854775808 / -1, which does not fit in 64 bits.
  • CAST(x AS BIGINT) of NaN, ±∞ or a huge double, also after ROUND.
  • Integer POWER with a negative exponent or a huge result.
  • A regular expression that does not compile.
  • Truncating a timestamp near the ends of its range to a month or year.
  • +, -, * leaving the declared width (64 bits for BIGINT). The reference raises, and so do the DuckDB and Polars translations.
  • An integer SUM leaving 64 bits. Sverify rules it out where the plan bounds a group's rows (a FETCH count) and requires bounds the column. Elsewhere it assumes each sum fits, and the job checks it on the data before the run (Report.assumed).
Lean's model computes with exact integers, and analysis/Sverify/Analysis/Safety.lean lists, for every operation of a plan, which of these can happen. Theorem Rel.mayIssues_sound proves the list complete: if the report lists no error, no input can trigger one. @sv.transform refuses a transformation that may fail, even with no postconditions.

Guards

The usual fix is a guard that keeps the divisor away from zero. Whether a guard works depends on when the engine evaluates each part. The variants below cover a zero divisor, MIN divided by -1 and doubles a BIGINT cannot hold. Pick one, and we'll read Lean's report.

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='pHFh-0' random-id='496a35eb-8a31-c55b-dc38-92d43a0eb21f'><marimo-dropdown data-initial-value='["qty // n (no guard)"]' data-label='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003epipeline\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-options='["qty // n (no guard)","filter n != 0, then select qty // n","filter n \u003e 0, then select qty // n","select qty % nullif(n, 0)","select CASE WHEN n != 0 THEN qty % n ELSE 0 END","filter (n != 0) AND (qty % n \u003e 1)","filter n != 0, then filter qty % n \u003e 1","select round(amount) (a cast to BIGINT)","filter 0 \u003c= amount \u003c= 100, then round(amount)","select qty + 1"]' data-allow-select-none='false' data-searchable='false' data-full-width='false' data-disabled='false'></marimo-dropdown></marimo-ui-element>

NOT proved: 2 preconditions needed
semantics: reference
postcondition status
needs ❌ (.qty >= -9 * 10**18) and (.n != 0) on t, inferred from qty // n (overflow or division by zero otherwise): declare them in requires (each run then checks them on the data), or rewrite so no row needs them (t.filter((_.qty >= -9 * 10**18) & (_.n != 0)) first, or a CASE); on_inferred='warn' assumes them instead
output column known values
x any integer or NULL

data.text/markdown:
What the variants show:
  • nullif(n, 0) and CASE are guards. The engines evaluate a CASE branch only when its condition holds, NULLIF is a CASE underneath, and Lean evaluates each branch knowing its condition.
  • A filter below a projection guards too, because the projection only sees rows that passed. n != 0 leaves MIN / -1 open, and n > 0 closes it.
  • The same AND is no guard: DuckDB and Polars evaluate both operands, so qty % n runs on the n = 0 row (eager AND and OR). The report flags the error inside the AND and suggests guarding the operation itself with the CASE above.
  • An earlier filter is no guard either. An optimizer may merge the two filters into one AND. Lean models that (Rel.loose) and reports the error.
  • round(amount) becomes a cast to BIGINT, which fails on 1e30 and NaN. Bounding amount first makes it safe, because ROUND is exact and monotone in the model (FloatCode.round_mono).
  • qty + 1 may fail on MAX, where the result does not fit in 64 bits and the reference raises. A precondition such as qty < 1000 rules it out.
A contracted transformation has to be proved free of runtime errors, and correctness on the inputs that happen to arrive does not count. We pass on_inferred="off" to ratio to see the error itself: by default Sverify works out the precondition (_.n != 0) and reports the plan as not proved until you declare it in requires. Declared, it is checked on each batch before the run, so report.run and refresh refuse a batch with n = 0 with a PreconditionError and nothing runs. A SUM that may overflow, or an operation on doubles that may overflow to ±∞, does not block the proof: the assumption is listed in Report.assumed and checked at run time, on the data before the run.

Report.errors lists the issues a proof has to rule out. Report.proved is true when every postcondition is proved and there are no errors. The timing of evaluation is trusted: when an engine evaluates an expression (lazy CASE, eager AND/OR, merged filters, and the constant conditions DuckDB evaluates while it plans the query). A constant that raises, such as 1 // 0 = 1 in a later WHEN, makes Sverify report the whole plan as raising, on any data. The test suite runs plans on random data, extreme values included, and checks that they fail only where Lean reported an error.

Windows and ASOF joins

Say the maintenance team asks how long each sensor went quiet between readings, because a long silence marks a unit to replace before it fails. Each reading needs the one before it. SQL looks at neighbouring rows with window functions: 
LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY sensor ORDER BY ts)
This reads: for each row, the ts of the previous row of the same sensor, in ts order, and NULL for the first one. The model supports LAG, LEAD and ROW_NUMBER with any sort direction, NULLs first or last, offsets and defaults (core/Sverify/Core/Window.lean).

Ibis numbers rows from 0. Lean knows that LAG(ts) comes from an earlier row of the same partition, so prev_ts <= ts, that a lagged partition column equals the row's own, and that ROW_NUMBER() is never negative. The first row's NULL is guarded with isnull() | … in the contract below.

Ties

Sensors sometimes report twice in the same instant. If two readings of a sensor share a ts, SQL does not say which is previous. The engine picks, and may pick differently on the next run, so Lean proves only what holds for every pick. Unless requires gives a key on the partition and order columns, report.deterministic is False and report.ties names the key that would close the ties. With the key, earlier means strictly earlier: prev_ts < ts.

data.text/markdown: Theorem window_tiebreak (analysis/Sverify/Analysis/Keys.lean) makes the keyed case trustworthy: when a window's partition and sort columns contain a key of its input, every way of sorting the input by the window's keys gives the same rows. The proof therefore describes what the engine computes, however it breaks ties. A run can ask for more: report.run(con, engine, reproducible=sv.equivalent()) refuses a plan whose result a rerun may change, and names the key that would fix it. We'll take the largest order, where two orders tie on the amount:

console.name: stdout
console.text: RouteError: refused on duckdb: a rerun must give the same result: the result is not determined up to row order: the deterministic profile needs a total order, and ties stay open at the fetch at relation 0: the rows it takes tie in ORDER BY [$2], with no key among those columns, so no rerun is sure to reproduce it; declare `unique(...)` on the partition (or grouping) and order columns of the input, or give first(), last() and windows a total order

data.text/markdown: The fix is the one the refusal names: a key in the order. With id as the tiebreak and sv.key("id") in requires, the result is determined, and the run goes ahead:

ASOF joins

An accelerometer samples at 100 Hz and a gyroscope at 130 Hz, so their timestamps rarely line up. To train a model on both, each accelerometer sample needs the latest gyroscope sample at or before it, and only if that one is recent enough. This is an ASOF join. Not every engine has one, and Ibis's asof_join compiles to DuckDB syntax, so sv.asof_join builds it from parts Lean understands: a range join, then ROW_NUMBER to keep the latest match. A gyroscope reading from the future would leak information the model cannot have in production. The contract states what an ASOF join promises: one output row per accelerometer sample, no gyroscope sample from the future, and none older than the tolerance.

data.text/html:
proved
semantics: reference
postcondition status
unique(device, ts) ✅ proved
(_.ts_right.isnull() | (_.ts_right <= _.ts)) ✅ proved
ts_right IS NULL OR ts_right >= ts - INTERVAL '10 milliseconds' ✅ proved
output column known values
device any integer
ts any timestamp
a any double or NULL
ts_right any timestamp or NULL
g any double or NULL

data.text/markdown:
Two things to try.
  • Lower the tolerance below 8 ms. The gyroscope samples every 7.7 ms, so some accelerometer samples find no partner. With how="left" they stay with NULLs, with "inner" they disappear, and the proofs hold either way.
  • Drop the key on gyr. Two gyroscope readings at the same instant tie for "latest". The guarantees hold for either one, and the result is not deterministic: a rerun may pair the sample with the other reading.
One row per sample comes from the key analysis: ROW_NUMBER() over a partition is a key together with the partition columns, and the filter rank = 0 drops the rank from that key. Framed window aggregates (AVG(v) OVER (ROWS 5 PRECEDING)), RANK and running sums verify too (Ibis coverage).

Composing contracts

Say the billing team owns a step that cleans up orders, and you own the step after it, which doubles the amounts for a promotion. You have never read their code and you should not have to. If a negative amount slips past them, your step doubles it and your name is on the incident. What you rely on is their contract. When the input of a contracted function is the result of another contracted function, sverify proves the downstream preconditions from the upstream contract, so the intermediate data is never checked. It also proves the downstream postconditions from what the upstream step guarantees, whatever its code happens to do.

data.text/html:
proved
semantics: reference
postcondition status
(_.doubled >= 0) ✅ proved
_.doubled.notnull() ✅ proved
output column known values
id any integer or NULL
customer a string or NULL
doubled an integer in [0, 1999999998]

data.text/markdown:
The requires paid: … rows show what doubled_paid was allowed to assume: the guarantees of paid. Each link is a Hoare triple, the notation of program verification: {P} f {Q} means that if P holds before f, then Q holds after. The rule
{P} g {Q} and {Q} f {S} give {P} f ∘ g {S}
is theorem Triple.compose in SubstraitLean/Compose.lean.

When the link breaks

We'll swap the upstream step for one that promises less. Pick what feeds doubled_paid.

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='mWxS-0' random-id='586a2308-bc44-3472-d17c-fd38181edb31'><marimo-radio data-initial-value='"not_null (guarantees only that amount is not NULL)"' data-label='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003eupstream step\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-options='["paid (guarantees amount ≥ 0 and not NULL)","not_null (guarantees only that amount is not NULL)","a plain Ibis filter: amount \u003e 0","a plain Ibis filter: amount IS NOT NULL"]' data-inline='false' data-disabled='false'></marimo-radio></marimo-ui-element>

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003eCompositionError: doubled_paid needs (\u003cem\u003e.amount &gt;= 0) (it may be FALSE on some rows), (\u003c/em\u003e.amount &lt; 1000000000) (it may be FALSE on some rows) on 't'; not_null only guarantees _.amount.notnull()\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"danger"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
• not_null guarantees too little: doubled_paid needs amount ≥ 0 and nothing upstream promises it. The error names both sides of the broken link. Only the contract counts, even though not_null's code would happen to keep negative amounts.
  • A plain Ibis step carries no contract, and what follows from its operations is still proved: amount > 0 implies both preconditions of doubled_paid. With only amount IS NOT NULL, the missing amount ≥ 0 is treated like a precondition on a base table: checked on the data if there is data, assumed otherwise.
  • A precondition can follow from more than the upstream ensures. It is then proved as an extra postcondition of the upstream function, from that function's own preconditions. Keys (sv.unique) propagate the same way.
On bound tables only the base tables are checked: paid's preconditions on orders. The intermediate result is never inspected, because doubled_paid's preconditions were proved.

Handing the contract to another team

The billing team may run its steps on an engine sverify doesn't drive. to_substrait() writes the proved plan as Substrait, which any conforming consumer runs, with the contract inside it: the preconditions the consumer must meet, the postconditions it may rely on, and a manifest of how the proof reaches Substrait. We'll export paid and read it back, which proves its contract again:

The class exact says a consumer that follows Substrait's spec gives the reference's rows. Where the spec leaves a choice open that the proof needs, the export says so and refuses: Substrait doesn't say how upper treats non-ASCII text (ST-10 on the upstream ledger), and the refusal names the way out:

console.name: stdout
console.text: ExportError: upper maps non-ASCII text by a rule Substrait leaves open (ST-10, upstream/bugs/ST-10.json); report.to_sql(dialect) writes the proved plan for an engine instead

data.text/markdown: A team that keeps its contracts in a data catalog rather than beside the plan reads them as ODCS, the Open Data Contract Standard. sverify.odcs writes a node's contract as an ODCS document, with the proved guarantees as its schema and quality rules, and reads one back as conditions for the next team's requires. We'll run paid over a small source, export the node's contract, and read it back:

You can now put a contract on a transformation and read what Lean proved about every column. You can prove keys and relations between columns, rule out the runtime errors that page people at night, pin down windows and ASOF joins, and chain steps from different teams with every link proved. The billing job gets a column whose promises were proved before any data ran, and the assumptions about upstream data are checked when the data arrives. Orders keep arriving, though. Next up is Pipelines and engines, where a contracted result is kept up to date from its changes, stored in Delta and Iceberg, and run on other engines.
